newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican goes against U.S. with Libya ties.
newsitem.headline: Vatican goes against U.S. with Libya ties.

text.p: In a move that put it at odds with the United States and other countries that have tried to isolate Col Muammar Gaddafi, the Vatican on Monday established full diplomatic relations with Libya.
Ambassadorial-level ties were forged despite months of what diplomatic sources called intense but private lobbying by the United States to convince the Holy See to hold back.

Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Vatican, which has diplomatic relations with more than 130 countries, had decided to forge ties with Tripoli in part to recognise recent "positive results" in Libya in the area of religious freedom.
Navarro-Valls said he hoped international reaction to the Vatican's decision would be positive.
He said the move was aimed primarily to more adequately look after the needs of the some 50,000 Catholics in the country Washington and Britain have accused of sponsoring terrorism.
Both have accused Libya of harbouring two suspects blamed for the 1988 bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland.
The United Nations also has imposed an air travel ban to Libya over the Lockerbie case.

The Vatican spokesman said the Holy See also hoped the decision would give a "particular impulse" to international dialogue and underscore its view that the Mediterranean should be "a region of peace, stability and security".
"The Catholic Church...wants to offer its sincere collaboration to this brotherly work," Navarro-Valls said, adding that he hoped the ties would help Christian-Moslem relations.
Diplomatic sources said Washington had been talking to the Vatican for some time about its concern over the impending relations.

"They (the U.S.) told them that they thought that it was not a good idea, that the United States was very concerned about support for terrorism and the suspicion that Libya is seeking to acquire weapons of mass destruction," a diplomatic source said.

The source added, however, that there was no attempt to pressure the Vatican or lay out any counter-measures and that Washington was now hopeful that the Holy See could exercise "a moderating influence" on Tripoli.
The Vatican and the United States have had diplomatic relations since 1984.
Last month, after the Vatican denied that Washington had issued a protest to the Holy See over impending relations, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said:

"We believe in general that it is best to isolate Libya because of Libya's direct support for terrorist groups, because of the fact that we believe there's very good reason to believe that two Libyan agents placed a bomb on board Pam Am flight 103 in December 1988 and killed 268 people," Burns said.
In 1992, during the height of the Lockerbie crisis, the Vatican bluntly told Libya to shun terrorism.
A year later the Vatican newspaper took a stand against U.N. sanctions against Libya over the Lockerbie case.
The new relations with Libya were the latest a series of Vatican moves in the past few years to strengthen ties with the Arab world after the Holy See recognised Israel in 1993.
The Vatican said Pope John Paul had appointed Archbishop Jose Sebastian Laboa as the Vatican's nuncio, or ambassador, to Libya.

Laboa is no stranger to controversy with the United States. He was the Pope's ambassador in Panama City when strongman General Manuel Antonio Noriega took refuge in the Vatican mission in 1989 to elude a U.S. invasion force.
The episode sent U.S.-Vatican relations plunging to one of their worst levels ever.
